item.title: Boulder Market Meals: Smoky chipotle meatballs with locally raised beef
item.dc:creator: John Lehndorff and Katie MacKinnon, Boulder County Farmers Markets
item.description:
Market Meals is a collaboration between Boulder Reporting Lab and the Boulder County Farmers Markets, featuring weekly seasonal recipes built around ingredients from local growers, ranchers and food producers. Find it in Nibbles every Tuesday and on Boulder Reporting Lab. Sign up to get Nibbles in your inbox. All season long in this recipe series, […]

The post Boulder Market Meals: Smoky chipotle meatballs with locally raised beef appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.
item.content:encoded:
Market Meals is a collaboration between Boulder Reporting Lab and the Boulder County Farmers Markets, featuring weekly seasonal recipes built around ingredients from local growers, ranchers and food producers. Find it in Nibbles every Tuesday and on Boulder Reporting Lab. Sign up to get Nibbles in your inbox.

All season long in this recipe series, we have highlighted local produce as it comes in and out of season. However, some local foods remain constant at the farmers market from April through November. One of those is protein — the beef, bison, chicken, pork and more that local ranchers bring to the Boulder and Longmont markets.

Just like knowing your vegetable farmer allows you to feel confident in the food you are eating, knowing your rancher does the same. You can learn where the animals are being raised, what they are eating and how they are being processed. And, if you’re lucky, you might be able to visit them and their animals on their land.

In our 40th season of running farmers markets here at Boulder County Farmers Markets, we have been hosting field trips to some of the farms represented at our farmers markets. Attendees get the chance to take a tour, ask questions and truly get to know their farmer.

A few weeks ago, our field trip program took us to Grama Grass & Livestock, which brings beef to the Boulder Farmers Market each week. The team at Grama Grass has a unique model: It grazes cattle on public and private property in a way that sequesters carbon in the soil, reduces the impact of drought and mitigates fire damage. These beneficial byproducts of its ranching practices are things you may only learn about by talking to the ranchers directly.

After the field trip, attendees sampled grass-finished meat from Grama Grass & Livestock cattle, including the chipotle meatball recipe we are sharing this week. Chipotle peppers are dried and smoked whole red jalapeño chilies. This recipe calls for canned chipotles in a thick tomato and vinegar adobo sauce.

Chipotle Meatballs

Meatballs

  • 1 pound Grama Grass ground beef
  • 1 large egg
  • ¼ cup uncooked white rice
  • About 5 mint leaves, finely chopped
  • 1 medium yellow onion, finely chopped
  • 3 large garlic cloves, minced
  • Salt and pepper, to taste
  • Vegetable oil, for cooking

Sauce

  • 1 (12-ounce) can tomato sauce
  • 1 (7-ounce) can chipotle chilies in adobo sauce
  • ½ medium yellow onion, peeled and finely chopped
  • 3 large garlic cloves, peeled and minced
  • 2 bay leaves
  • Salt, to taste

Add the tomato sauce, chipotle peppers, onion and garlic to a blender. Blend until smooth. Set the sauce aside, keeping the bay leaves separate.

In a large bowl, combine the beef, egg, uncooked rice, mint, onion, garlic, salt and pepper. Mix until all the ingredients are evenly incorporated. Shape the mixture into meatballs of your preferred size, keeping them similar in size so they cook evenly.

Heat a small amount of oil in a large, deep skillet with a lid over medium heat. Add the meatballs and cook for about 3 minutes, turning them so they brown on all sides. Pour the blended sauce over the meatballs and add the bay leaves.

Bring the sauce to a gentle simmer. Cover the skillet with the lid and cook over medium-low heat for approximately 45 minutes, or until the meatballs are fully cooked and the rice is tender. Do not stir, as the meatballs may fall apart.

Remove the bay leaves before serving. Taste the sauce and add salt if needed.

What’s fresh this week? Farmers are bringing lettuce, greens, pears, melons, summer squash, potatoes, eggplant, peppers, sweet corn, tomatoes, green beans, okra, chilies, carrots, garlic, apples and more to the Boulder Farmers Market and the Longmont Farmers Market this week.

Visiting the Markets

Boulder Farmers Market

  • 13th Street between Arapahoe Ave. and Canyon Blvd.
  • 8 a.m.-2 p.m., Saturdays, April 4-Nov. 21; 3:30-7:30 p.m., Wednesdays, May 6-Oct. 7
  • More information

Longmont Farmers Market

  • Boulder County Fairgrounds
  • 8 a.m.-1 p.m. Saturdays, April 4-Nov. 21
  • More information 

Have a tip or suggestion? Send your comments, questions and ideas to nibbles@boulderreportinglab.org.

item.title: BVSD says closing schools will help students. Families want more answers.
item.dc:creator: Jenna Sampson
item.description:
Ahead of a Sept. 22 vote, families are pressing for details about capacity, special education and long-term enrollment. District officials say some answers will not be available before the board acts.

The post BVSD says closing schools will help students. Families want more answers. appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.
item.content:encoded:
The morning after Boulder Valley School District proposed closing Douglass Elementary, special education teacher Lauren Dean drove to work on little sleep.

Staff learned of the proposal only the day before, alongside the rest of the community. Under the plan, Douglass’s attendance area would be divided among three elementary schools, and High Peaks would move into the Douglass building. When Dean arrived, she found the sidewalk covered in chalk drawings left by families: rainbows, hearts and messages of encouragement for teachers and their principal.

“There were a lot of tears that night for staff,” Dean said. “Most of us barely slept.”

The district had breakfast waiting for employees inside.

“Nobody had an appetite,” Dean said. “We were grateful for the coffee.”

The scene at Douglass captures the immediate disruption of a proposal BVSD unveiled Aug. 25 and says is necessary to protect the quality of education as enrollment declines. The plan would close four elementary schools — Douglass, Flatirons, Mesa and Birch — and trigger consolidations, program moves and grade-level changes at 12 others beginning in fall 2027. 

District leaders say operating fewer schools would allow them to provide smaller, more stable classes, richer programming and more consistent staffing.  

But in the days since BVSD identified which schools would close, merge or move, families have begun scrutinizing the plan, with questions about projected class sizes, special education programs, resources at receiving schools and what happens to a neighborhood when it loses its school. Some of those questions, district officials say, will not be answered before the board votes.

Board of Education President Nicole Rajpal has said the board needs to move quickly to address declining enrollment. The board is scheduled to hear public comment on the proposal Sept. 8 and vote Sept. 22.

“Many of the other questions being asked are nearly impossible for me to answer with a high degree of confidence until the board votes on the proposal, we see where students enroll, and the state approves the School Finance Act for the 2027/28 school year,” Rajpal said in an email.

The district has also declined to provide the calculations behind some of its estimates, including its projection that the plan would save $3.5 million to $4 million a year.

“At this stage it would be premature to be more specific,” BVSD Communications Director Randy Barber told Boulder Reporting Lab when asked how the district calculated that figure. 

BVSD has said the savings would come primarily from reduced staffing and operating costs. 

How full is too full? 

In South Boulder, one open question is captured by the number 522.

That is how many resident students BVSD projects will live within the combined Mesa and Bear Creek attendance area by 2030. The Bear Creek building, where the two schools would be consolidated, has room for 492. Mesa’s RISE program for students with autism would also move there.

Yet BVSD projects that only 403 to 462 of those students will actually enroll, putting the school at 82% to 94% capacity. A footnote in the district’s presentation says the range depends on how many students from the sending school ultimately attend the receiving school. The projection assumes some children living in the attendance area will continue to attend other schools.

One Mesa parent asked whether the combined school could eventually exceed capacity, leaving less room for open-enrolled students, and whether Lifelong Learning enrichment classes and nearby preschool options would remain.

“I would love to hear the board address these concerns before voting,” the parent wrote in an email to Boulder Reporting Lab.

BVSD has since said preschool will remain available in South Boulder, with specific locations to be announced by Oct. 1. The district also says it can manage open enrollment to preserve space for resident students.

“Open enrollment processes are the levers in which we can use to make sure that schools fit inside their buildings,” Superintendent Rob Anderson said during the Aug. 31 Q&A. 

BVSD estimates the full proposal would require up to $10 million in facility modifications. The district has not released school-by-school renovation plans or cost estimates. 

“Staff conducted preliminary evaluations of building floor plans to determine what renovations/adjustments might be needed for enrollment and programming changes and to develop high-level, preliminary cost estimates,” BVSD said in a written response to Boulder Reporting Lab.

Districtwide, the proposal would reduce the number of schools with fewer than two classes per grade from 14 to six and increase building utilization from 68% to 75%. 

Questions about Douglass’s ICAN program 

At Douglass, parents and staff want more information about the proposed move of its Intensive Center for Affective Needs, or ICAN, program to Heatherwood Elementary. The center-based special education program serves students with intensive emotional and behavioral needs. At Douglass, 21% of students have individualized education programs, the highest share in the district.

Parents say the change could be particularly disruptive for students who rely on consistent staff, routines and surroundings.

“We cannot take an ableist approach that assumes disruption impacts every child equally,” said Rhonda McManus, the parent of a Douglass ICAN student. “Equity means recognizing those differences and considering our highest-needs students first.”

BVSD says students would continue to receive the services and transportation required by their individualized education programs. The district’s special education department would contact affected families, and receiving schools would receive transition support. Douglass families say those assurances do not answer their program-specific questions.

Could closing a school deepen the decline? 

BVSD’s proposal rests on data showing several years of declining enrollment and projections showing the trend continuing through 2030. Some families want the district to look further ahead, arguing that closing a school could shape a neighborhood long after those projections end. 

Four days before BVSD unveiled its plan, the City of Boulder and Boulder County gave final approval to an updated Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan. The 20-year vision calls for more housing choices, a more multigenerational city and walkable “15-minute neighborhoods.” It identifies attracting and retaining households with children as a community goal and acknowledges that having fewer children affects neighborhood vitality, public school funding and facilities. The plan does not itself change zoning or forecast a rebound in the number of children.

Flatirons families argue that closing a neighborhood school could make those goals harder to achieve by giving families with children one less reason to remain in or move to central Boulder. Under the proposal, students would be reassigned to Whittier or Foothill. Both schools are about a 40-minute walk from Flatirons.

Concerns like these have led some parents to ask the board to delay its Sept. 22 vote until the district provides more answers and longer-term analysis. 

“University Hill is already struggling to retain families amid Boulder’s housing costs, investor ownership and neighborhood turnover,” University Hill Neighborhood Association President Elise Longbottom said. “Flatirons is one of the remaining pieces of civic infrastructure anchoring families to the neighborhood.”

BVSD said the comprehensive plan is unlikely to materially change enrollment in the near future. 

“Changes to the comprehensive plan primarily apply to infill development proposals with only a limited capacity to significantly impact enrollment within BVSD for the foreseeable future,” Barber said. 

Whether closing a school would accelerate the loss of families from Boulder is difficult to establish. School access is only one factor in where families live, alongside housing costs, birth rates and household size. 

Longer-term enrollment is also a question in South Boulder, where CU Boulder’s plans for its CU South property could include up to 1,100 housing units for faculty, staff and non-first-year students. Under BVSD’s proposed attendance boundaries, students living there would be assigned to Bear Creek.

BVSD said it has not met with CU Boulder officials about the development. The university’s plans are still taking shape, and more housing does not necessarily produce more students. But families cite the project as one reason they want enrollment projections extending beyond 2030.

‘There’s not a plan B’ 

BVSD’s proposal would not take effect until the 2027-28 school year, giving the district nearly a year to manage moves and transitions. Families, however, have only weeks to scrutinize the plan and press for answers before the board votes.

“There’s not a plan B. This is the proposal,” Anderson said during the Aug. 31 Q&A. 

Some parents question whether public feedback can still change it.

“I feel frustrated they are going through the motions of giving us 45 minutes of public comments when [the board and district] are clearly in lockstep with each other, so it’s for show,” Flatirons parent Elaine Ellis said. “But in the meanwhile, I don’t feel that I’m getting the information I need from the administration and board to start making a major decision.”

Rajpal has maintained that she does not know how the board will vote, but said the proposal meets the requirements the board established at the outset. 

Meanwhile, teachers at Douglass had to begin navigating the proposal’s consequences less than 12 hours after learning their school could close. 

After parents left the sidewalk that morning, teachers gathered students into classroom circles.

“Students cried. Students expressed anger,” Dean said.

By the end of the school day, some students had begun making protest posters. At dismissal, Dean said, they gathered outside and chanted: “Save our school.”

The post BVSD says closing schools will help students. Families want more answers. appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.

item.title: Boulder City Council honors Mark Wallach in emotional farewell after resignation
item.dc:creator: Brooke Stephenson
item.description:
Former Boulder Councilmember Mark Wallach, who resigned in July, was honored by his former colleagues during the Sept. 3 council meeting. “One thing I appreciated so much about you as a colleague was that you always said and did what you believed to be right,” Councilmember Nicole Speer said before reading a declaration in his […]

The post Boulder City Council honors Mark Wallach in emotional farewell after resignation appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.
item.content:encoded:
Former Boulder Councilmember Mark Wallach, who resigned in July, was honored by his former colleagues during the Sept. 3 council meeting.

“One thing I appreciated so much about you as a colleague was that you always said and did what you believed to be right,” Councilmember Nicole Speer said before reading a declaration in his honor. “I’m not sure that you have a political bone in your body, unless they snuck one in with your new hip.”

Wallach, 73, resigned in protest over the council’s decision to keep Boulder Municipal Airport open indefinitely. He is also recovering from a recent hip fracture.

Wallach is known for his candor and dry, often self-deprecating sense of humor. Speer praised his respect for city staff, commitment to honesty and transparency, and dedication to thoroughly reading each council packet. During his time on council, Wallach also became known for his deeply considered posts on the Boulder City Council Hotline, where he frequently poked fun at himself and the length of his messages.

“For those of you who have yearned for another Hotline from me, your wishes are hereby granted,” Wallach began one such email this April. “For those who would rather not hear from me at all, my sincere condolences.”

Wallach received a standing ovation in the council chambers Thursday night.

Wallach grew emotional as he addressed the room, calling his time on council “an experience of a lifetime.”

“I think my only regret is that I came to council very late in life, and my parents never got to see it,” he said. “I think they would have been proud of me.”

Wallach also thanked his wife. “Nothing I have done on council, or frankly anywhere else, could have been done without the support and love of my wife Joan,” he said. “Thank you for 40 years. It’s been wonderful. I could hope for 40 more years, but I try to be a realist.”

“That was amazing, Mark,” Mayor Aaron Brockett said, wiping his eyes. “I laughed, I cried. You will be deeply missed up here, but we’re very excited for your next act.”

The post Boulder City Council honors Mark Wallach in emotional farewell after resignation appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.

item.title: Boulder County’s ponds are drying up. Officials can’t simply refill them.
item.dc:creator: Por Jaijongkit
item.description:
Extreme drought has shrunk ponds and wetlands, causing fish kills and foul odors. Officials often lack the water rights or infrastructure to refill them, though a county wildlife official says the damage is likely temporary.

The post Boulder County’s ponds are drying up. Officials can’t simply refill them. appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.
item.content:encoded:
At Walden Ponds east of Boulder, receding water has left dead fish along the shoreline. Similar conditions are visible within city limits at Viele Lake in South Boulder and at a pond along Wonderland Creek in the northeast Kings Ridge neighborhood, where carp lie dead in stagnant, algae-filled water.

Across Boulder County’s plains, extreme drought is shrinking small lakes, ponds and wetlands. In some places, falling water levels have caused fish kills and foul odors. The damage can look permanent. 

But city and county officials say many of these habitats are likely to recover when wetter conditions return. The immediate problem is that, even as the ponds dry, officials cannot simply refill them. 

Many of the affected water bodies are artificial, including former mining pits that now depend largely on rain, runoff and groundwater. Some have no infrastructure through which water could be delivered. In other cases, the city or county lacks the legal right to divert scarce water into them. 

Late-summer drying is not unusual. Hot weather increases evaporation, and shallow ponds and wetlands routinely lose water. This year, however, the effects have been magnified by prolonged heat and record-low snowpack, which have reduced runoff and groundwater recharge, according to the City of Boulder. 

No water to send

Only about 20% of the wetlands managed by the city receive some water through irrigation, city spokesperson Jennifer Ciplet said. Many others have no delivery system connecting them to a water source. 

“The city does not have a water source, a control mechanism, or a water right to fill these,” Ciplet said. 

Colorado’s water rights system gives priority to those who began using water first. When a senior water user places a call, users with more junior rights may have to stop diverting water until the senior right is satisfied. 

The current call on Boulder Creek extends to water rights dating to 1860, said Jeff Moline, Boulder County’s agricultural water specialist. That means rights established after 1860 are too junior to receive water under current conditions. 

The City of Boulder holds some water rights dating to 1850 and is using them to maintain certain water bodies, including the Kids Fishing Pond in downtown Boulder, Ciplet said. The city is also using water to support flows in Boulder Creek. 

Many smaller water bodies have far more junior water rights. They include a pond along Wonderland Creek in the Kings Ridge neighborhood. Walden Ponds, just east of Boulder, has water rights dating only to 2002.  

“It’s way, way, way down in priority. We don’t have any water that we can send into Walden Ponds,” Moline said. 

Although the county received some rain earlier in the summer, it was not enough to replenish the groundwater that feeds many of these water bodies, Moline said.

Conditions vary across the county. Pella Crossing, near Hygiene and west of Longmont, remains healthy because it receives fresh groundwater. Larger lakes and reservoirs are also generally being maintained. 

City and county wetland regulations are intended to protect these environments from pollution, development and other human disturbances, not fluctuations in weather. 

“It is not a violation of city code for a pond or wetland to experience lower water levels or be temporarily dry due to natural environmental conditions such as drought,” Ciplet said. 

The strain extends beyond Boulder County. Colorado Parks and Wildlife has imposed dozens of drought-related restrictions and closures and is monitoring ecosystems where drought has complicated recovery after wildfires. 

Denver Water closed Antero Reservoir to recreation for the season so its water could be redirected. Colorado Parks and Wildlife also authorized an emergency fish salvage at Westminster’s shrinking McKay Lake. Earlier this year, Boulder County farmers scaled back crops, staffing and community-supported agriculture programs because of the drought. 

Ugly, but not necessarily permanent

Despite the visible stress, Mac Kobza, Boulder County’s wildlife management supervisor, said he has not seen evidence that the drought is causing irreversible damage to the lakes or their wildlife. 

“In many ecosystems around the world, drought is a natural cycle,” said Kobza, who has worked in wildlife management for 26 years and specializes in aquatic ecosystems. 

Many of the shrinking ponds are artificial and do not support the complex ecosystems found in natural lakes and wetlands. They are often populated by fish species such as largemouth bass, common carp and catfish. 

Those ponds can struggle with low oxygen even during an ordinary summer. As temperatures rise and bacteria consume organic matter, oxygen levels fall, sometimes killing fish. 

Removing dead or struggling fish is not necessarily better for the ecosystem, Kobza said, because it also removes nutrients that would otherwise feed insects, birds and other animals. 

This year’s fish kills have provided food for invertebrates and birds, including bald eagles, Kobza said. Other birds can move to larger lakes where prey remains available. Drying ponds can also suppress invasive bullfrogs, which spread disease to native amphibians and are notoriously difficult to remove. 

“Disturbance is part of an ecological process,” Kobza said. “These are the natural forces that regulate populations of wildlife and create opportunities.” 

Native species are generally adapted to periods of drought and can retreat to remaining refuges until conditions improve, Kobza said. Unless creeks remain critically dry for an extended period, he expects most populations to recover.

“I haven’t, at this point, really had an indication that we’re seeing damage to the ecosystem where we’re losing native wildlife,” he said.

In many cases, Kobza said, the best option is to let nature run its course. 

“There isn’t much we can do to stop it, especially in a high drought situation,” he said. 

That can be difficult for residents confronted with dead fish, shrinking ponds and strong odors. 

“I get the smell and the look is very bad. I understand that, but it is generally temporary,” Kobza said. 

For now, the outlook for the affected ponds depends largely on the weather. More rain could begin replenishing groundwater, streams and floodplains. A stronger winter snowpack could improve runoff and water supplies next year. 

“Hopefully we can start in a different spot next year,” Moline said. 

The post Boulder County’s ponds are drying up. Officials can’t simply refill them. appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.

item.title: Boulder County’s starring role in the 1966 ‘Stagecoach’ remake
item.dc:creator: Silvia Pettem
item.description:
The star-studded 1966 remake of the iconic 1939 western “Stagecoach” was filmed at Silver Lake, along the Switzerland Trail and at the Blue Bird Mine complex.

The post Boulder County’s starring role in the 1966 ‘Stagecoach’ remake appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.
item.content:encoded:
Sixty years ago, 20th Century Fox released the 1966 remake of the 1939 film “Stagecoach.” The original John Ford classic starred John Wayne as an outlaw and Claire Trevor as a prostitute. The new version starred Alex Cord and Ann-Margret, along with a slew of supporting stars that included singer Bing Crosby and comedian Red Buttons. 

Much of the first “Stagecoach” was filmed in Monument Valley, Utah. Before production began, the producer told a Boulder reporter that he was “planning a greener, more refreshing type picture than the dusty original.” True to his word, many of the scenes were filmed in western Boulder County. 

The late Alan Cass, whose grandparents, Fred and Edith White, owned some of the properties where the film was shot, kept meticulous notes on the local scenes. Recognizing these scenes, and knowing something of their history, makes the film fun to watch today.

The plot revolves around the stagecoach’s seven passengers. All had compelling reasons to leave the fictional town of Dry Forks. After stunning aerial shots that sweep over Fourth of July Canyon (west of the town of Eldora), the cast is introduced when the “Law and Order League” kicks out the prostitute and an alcoholic doctor. 

The others include a pregnant Army wife intent on reuniting with her husband, a belligerent banker who had stolen a payroll, a gambler intent on protecting the Army wife, and a timid whiskey salesman whose “samples” disappeared into the hands and belly of the doctor. The outlaw Ringo Kid (picked up at North Boulder Falls) was determined to find the men who murdered his family. Buck, a nervous stage driver, and Curly, a marshal, rode on top.

Filmed in 1965, the 1966 version includes scenes on dirt roads near Silver Lake (off-limits to the public, as it’s within the City of Boulder’s watershed). Instead of the rock formations of Monument Valley, our own Arapaho Peaks and Arapaho Glacier are in the background.

Movie watchers will also glimpse the railroad grade of the Switzerland Trail. The location was an easy choice for the producer, as the grade was free of electrical lines and appropriate for the early 1870s era. 

In the film, the stagecoach stops at the Blue Bird Mine complex, just as the railroad did in the early 1900s. The mine, discovered in 1871, was primarily known for its silver. The name “Blue Bird” came from blue azurite, a copper mineral found in the silver ore. 

Beginning in 1905, after the Switzerland Trail was extended south to the town of Eldora, the Blue Bird stop (only a platform, not a station) was a destination for excursionists who spent hours gathering wildflowers and hiking to the waterfall on North Boulder Creek. Now, the mine complex is part of Boulder County’s Caribou Ranch Open Space.

Although the mines at the Blue Bird site are not part of the 1966 film “Stagecoach,” the still-standing bunkhouse was used as the passengers’ first stage stop. The scene is pivotal, as it is there that the stage’s cavalry escort turns back, leaving the passengers on their own to face the threat of an attack by the Sioux (or, in the 1939 film, the Apache). Even so, all of the passengers agree to continue on to their destination.

Only the exterior of the building was shot on location. The interior scenes were filmed in a Hollywood studio, with large photos placed in the windows to show the landscape outside.

Caribou Ranch Open Space (not to be confused with the townsite of Caribou, farther west) was formerly the Tucker Ranch. The Van Vleet family purchased it in 1936. The property became known as the Lazy VV Ranch, where the Van Vleets raised Arabian horses. The site was also used as a backdrop for Warner Bros. westerns and shorts during the 1940s, including “Arabians of the Rockies” and “Sons of Courage.”

In 1971, music producer, songwriter and director James W. Guercio purchased the ranch and opened the Caribou Ranch Recording Studio. It was severely damaged by fire in 1985. Boulder County purchased the ranch (including the Blue Bird complex) in 2002 and landmarked the properties in 2004. 

Both the 1939 and 1966 versions of “Stagecoach” contain conflicts with Native Americans. The later version has been criticized for its depictions of Native Americans as “savages.” (The first confrontation is on Caribou Ranch property.) Both films are available online. A 2000 review called the 1966 version a “colorful star-studded western” that “can’t hold a candle to the 1939 masterpiece.” 

The trailhead to Caribou Ranch is in Sherwood Gulch, off CO 72, north of Nederland. The Blue Bird Mine complex (including the bunkhouse) is accessible to hikers on the “Bluebird Loop.”

The post Boulder County’s starring role in the 1966 ‘Stagecoach’ remake appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.

item.title: Ty Haney and Katie Wolf: BVSD should prove school closures are the best option
item.dc:creator: Opinion
item.description:
Declining enrollment is real. But before closing neighborhood elementary schools, the district should publicly model less destructive alternatives and explain why they would not work.

The post Ty Haney and Katie Wolf: BVSD should prove school closures are the best option  appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.
item.content:encoded:
This commentary is by Ty Haney and Katie Wolf, parents and members of the Flatirons Elementary School community.

A neighborhood elementary school is more than a building where kids learn to read. It is the beating heart of a neighborhood.  

It is where children walk to school in the morning. Where parents meet one another. Where friendships form among families who live blocks apart. It is a playground, a gathering place and an anchor connecting generations of neighbors.

Closing a neighborhood school is like ripping the heart out of a neighborhood.  

The Boulder Valley School District recently proposed closing four neighborhood elementary schools in response to declining enrollment. In doing so, the district is asking us to accept a simple premise: Enrollment is declining, so neighborhood schools must close.

Under BVSD’s Aug. 25 proposal, the district would close Birch, Douglass, Mesa and Flatirons elementary schools. District officials say consolidation would reduce empty seats and give schools a fuller complement of teachers, counselors and programs. But closing schools is not the only way to achieve those goals. 

Declining enrollment is real, but school closures are not inevitable. They are a policy choice.

That doesn’t mean there is nothing to fix. Smaller schools can cost more per student, and uneven enrollment makes it harder to distribute teachers, specialists and programs equitably. But before the school board makes a decision this disruptive and irreversible, we should ask a more fundamental question: Have we exhausted less destructive ways to adapt?  

Start with the district’s own cost structure.

Our analysis of BVSD budgets over the last decade found that central administrative costs grew about 50% while enrollment declined about 10%. If the district has fewer students but substantially more bureaucracy, closing neighborhood schools should not be the first or only answer to the resulting financial pressure.

The proposed closures also need to be put in perspective. BVSD estimates the district would save approximately $3.5 million to $4 million annually, a small fraction of its overall budget, while one-time facility modifications could cost up to $10 million, plus transition costs. That’s very little savings for a lot of community heartbreak.

We’ve been down this road before. BVSD closed multiple schools in 2003. The district has never publicly disclosed to the community how much those closures saved. During an Aug. 31 livestream, however, Superintendent Rob Anderson said that, more than 20 years later, the district is still hearing about the fallout.

This isn’t unique to Boulder. A recent Stanford University study  found that school closures rarely bring the savings districts expect, especially when closures prompt students to leave the district entirely.   

There is another lever BVSD can pull: the enrollment system itself.

BVSD doesn’t simply send every child to the closest school. Neighborhood boundaries, open enrollment, focus programs and other policies influence where students go. The distribution of students among our schools isn’t purely an act of nature. It is something we designed.

And what we designed, we can redesign.

If one school is overcrowded while another nearby neighborhood school has empty seats, we can redraw boundaries. We can reform open enrollment. We can place attractive programs in under-enrolled schools. We can change how choice interacts with neighborhood enrollment. We can intentionally distribute students and resources more effectively across the district.

These options involve tradeoffs. But so does closing a school. 

Declining enrollment requires change. Pretending otherwise won’t help our children, teachers or taxpayers. But change does not automatically mean closure.

Before permanently removing the hearts of our neighborhoods, the district should show the community how the alternatives compare with the closure plan. What happens if we reduce administrative growth? What happens if we reform enrollment policies? Could a combination of approaches preserve neighborhood schools while addressing the district’s resource constraints?

Those scenarios should be modeled publicly and compared with closures in terms of finances, educational outcomes, transportation, community impact and long-term flexibility.  

Only then can the community understand the actual choices in front of us. 

The most dangerous idea in this debate is that we have no choice at all. 

We do.

Closing neighborhood schools is a choice. Before we make it, we’re asking BVSD to delay the vote and prove it is the best one. 

The post Ty Haney and Katie Wolf: BVSD should prove school closures are the best option  appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.

item.title: For 20 years, Bliss has brought Boulder artists and shoppers together. Now it’s fighting to stay open.
item.dc:creator: McKenzie Watson-Fore
item.description:
The locally owned gift and art boutique says rising costs and unpredictable spending threaten its future and the creative network it supports.

The post For 20 years, Bliss has brought Boulder artists and shoppers together. Now it’s fighting to stay open. appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.
item.content:encoded:
For more than two decades, Bliss has filled a Pearl Street storefront with local art, jewelry and offbeat gifts. To owner Hanna Harem, the boutique is part of what makes downtown Boulder feel like Boulder, rather than a shopping district that could be anywhere. 

Now, she says, the store is fighting to survive. Its struggle reflects broader pressures facing locally owned retailers downtown, including rising costs, unpredictable foot traffic and increasingly cautious consumers. 

Bliss’s sales fell nearly 37% in July compared with the same month last year. The decline did not follow an unusually strong period: Sales in 2025 were already lower than in 2024, according to Harem. 

“This isn’t simply a comparison to an unusually strong year,” Harem wrote in an email to Boulder Reporting Lab. “A nearly 37% decline in a single month is a substantial step backward and really illustrates the level of difficulty we’re facing right now.”

A Bliss employee launched a GoFundMe campaign on Harem’s behalf to help cover the store’s basic expenses and bills. As of Sept. 3, it had raised $2,093 toward a $16,000 goal. 

Inside, Bliss is part curio shop, part local arts hub and part vintage store. Gently used baby clothes hang across from vintage crystal wine glasses. Locally made backpacks sit beside a Colorado 14ers Summit Log and a guidebook to nearby hiking trails. Artwork covers the walls, with small placards introducing the artists behind it.

Founded in 2005 at 1643 Pearl St., Bliss began as a gift and home décor boutique. Harem joined the staff in 2011 and became its owner in 2020. Today, customers browse custom jewelry and accessories, quirky objets d’art, notebooks, gifts and home goods. 

Bliss also carries work by more than a dozen local artists and makers, including painters, jewelry designers, ceramicists and woodworkers. 

Painter Andrew Barker has sold his work through Bliss for the past six years. Bliss was the first store to carry his paintings and has given him another way to take part in Boulder’s visual arts scene.

“They’re really good about putting together events, allowing their artists to demonstrate process and interface with customers directly,” Barker said. 

Because Bliss draws tourists and other visitors, Barker said, it puts his paintings in front of people who might not otherwise encounter his work. 

“You get a lot of eyes on your work,” Barker said. 

Having a steady retail outlet also allows Barker to display and sell his work without taking time away from making it. 

“It’s really helpful to have a place where I can send people when they’re interested in my work,” Barker said. “My only other option is to have them come to my studio, which is often in use, and I have to schedule a time.”

The summer rebound has become harder to count on

For many retailers, winter is the slow season and summer offers a chance to recover. At Bliss, Harem said, that rebound has become harder to count on.

“The cost of operating here is high and continues to rise,” Harem told Boulder Reporting Lab, “while foot traffic and consumer spending have become less predictable each year.”

Rent is only one part of the cost of running a downtown shop. Bliss must also cover payroll, insurance, utilities, credit-card processing fees, taxes and inventory.

“There is very little room for a small business to have a slow month anymore,” Harem said, “and Bliss is experiencing more of those slow months. At this point, it’s fair to say that Bliss is fighting to keep its doors open.”

Harem said some customers browse in the store before buying online, while others are embracing social media trends built around “no-spend months.”

“For a small brick-and-mortar retailer, those broader shifts can have a very real cumulative impact,” she said.

Venus Sakha encountered similar pressures at Boulder Bazaar, the Nepalese and Tibetan gift shop she closed in August after nearly 20 years in business.

“Now, even when we do a discount, nobody wants to buy,” Sakha said. “They like it, but they say, ‘Oh, it’s very hard to afford.’”

John Tayer, president and CEO of the Boulder Chamber, said the pressures confronting retailers extend beyond Boulder. Inflation, import tariffs and higher labor costs are raising expenses just as consumers become more cautious.

“The consumer is more hesitant to spend,” Tayer said. “They’re equally as impacted by some of these broader economic conditions.”

“These are challenging times for our local independent businesses,” he added.

What a storefront contributes

For Harem, the stakes extend beyond her own business. Bliss sells work by local artists, makers and designers, so each purchase can support a wider creative network.

“When someone spends money at Bliss, they aren’t just supporting me as the business owner,” she said. “They’re supporting an entire network of local artists, makers, designers and other small businesses whose work fills the store. One purchase can have a ripple effect throughout our local creative community.”

The struggle at Bliss comes as several national brands open or prepare to open in prominent Boulder storefronts. Framebridge, a national custom-framing company, is preparing to open at 1640 Pearl St., formerly home to Pearl Convenience Market. The market relocated after its owners said proposed lease terms at the old location had become too expensive. Its move to 1711 Pearl St. put an end to an experiment in subsidized downtown space for local artists. 

Reformation, an upscale women’s clothing brand, has opened at 1142 Pearl St., while Peak Design, a luxury bag and outdoor gear company, is preparing to open a store in the 1600 block.

Those openings do not, on their own, show that chains are replacing local businesses throughout downtown. Tayer rejects the idea that independent businesses are disappearing.

“Downtown, we’re hovering around 70% or more local, independent businesses, and that’s characteristic of the entire community,” he said. “That provides great color and character to our retail and restaurant sectors, and that makes it really attractive for residents and visitors.”

But Harem worries that each independent store that disappears leaves downtown a little less distinctive.

“You can find the same chain stores in dozens or even hundreds of cities,” she said. “It’s the locally owned shops, restaurants and galleries, what you discover inside them and the experience you have visiting them, that makes you remember you were in Boulder.”

For now, Harem’s immediate goal is to keep Bliss open. Her longer view is about the kind of downtown that will remain for those who come next. 

“I want the next generation of Boulder residents and visitors to experience a downtown filled with businesses that could only exist here,” she added.

The post For 20 years, Bliss has brought Boulder artists and shoppers together. Now it’s fighting to stay open. appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.

item.title: At BMoCA, three artists turn family history into a conversation across generations
item.dc:creator: Rossana Longo-Better
item.description:
“Tres Voces, Un Corazón” brings together Sylvia Montero, Tony Ortega and their son, Cipriano Ortega, as the museum raises money for a new home in North Boulder.

The post At BMoCA, three artists turn family history into a conversation across generations appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.
item.content:encoded:
Visitors entering the Boulder Museum of Contemporary Art expecting a conventional family exhibition quickly discover something unexpected, in the best sense of the word. 

Superman wears the colors of the Mexican flag while leaping over a pre-Hispanic pyramid. Mickey Mouse becomes a Día de los Muertos piñata. The Statue of Liberty shares space with the Virgin of Guadalupe. Frida Kahlo appears alongside Snoopy and tacos.  

Nothing is placed where viewers expect it to be. That is precisely the point. 

“Tres Voces, Un Corazón,” guest-curated by Maruca Salazar, brings together the work of visual artists Tony Ortega and Sylvia Montero and their son, multidisciplinary artist and musician Cipriano Ortega. Together, they explore how identity, cultural memory and artistic language are inherited, questioned and reimagined across generations. 

The three artists have studios on different floors of their shared home, but each has a distinct voice. 

The exhibition comes as BMoCA plans an expansion.

The museum is raising $25 million for a new flagship building within the planned North Boulder Creative Campus. BMoCA says it has secured $13.6 million, or 54% of its goal, including an $800,000 commitment from a Boulder family and a $1.5 million award through a state tax credit program.

Near the entrance, photographs printed on handmade papel amate produced by Otomí artisans in Puebla, Mexico, connect the artists’ family roots in New Mexico with Indigenous traditions tied to earth and place. 

“I wanted it to tie into earth and land,” Tony Ortega said of the portraits that greet visitors.

Ortega’s work reflects the political and cultural legacy of the Chicano Movement through printmaking, painting and mixed-media installations. He describes his pieces as “hybrid images.” 

“I’m mixing Mexican and American culture,” Ortega said while walking through the exhibition. “Our culture is mixed, intertwined, juxtaposed, contrasted with American culture. It’s completely ingrained in all of us.”

Instead of separating cultures into opposing narratives, Ortega intentionally layers them. Superman becomes “Super Hombre.” Christian iconography appears alongside Indigenous pyramids. Familiar American imagery is reimagined through Mexican history and Chicano experience.

One installation, which Ortega said he created during the first Trump administration and later expanded in response to current immigration policies, layers Edvard Munch’s “The Scream” with the Virgin of Guadalupe mourning a child separated at the border. Nearby, monarch butterflies become symbols of migration.

“Borders don’t prevent them from migrating,” Ortega said. “Migrants come … for better lives, for their families and their communities.”

For Sylvia Montero, questioning inherited narratives has shaped more than three decades of artistic practice.

Standing before her wall-spanning installation, “They Came by Ships,” Montero reflected on the lasting consequences of colonization while drawing on her Mexican and Apache heritage.

“My father was born in the United States, but his brothers and sisters were born in Mexico,” she said, recalling family stories about crossing the Rio Grande as children. Those memories eventually became part of her artistic language.

“I’ve been painting since ’92, and I’m still talking about the same thing,” Montero said. “It gets tiring … but we have to still keep our strength and our hope.”

For Montero, resistance is less about confrontation than creation.

“Resistance is the healing,” she said. “When you create an art piece … you can share it with the world.”

Her son, Cipriano Ortega, works through music, theater, poetry and installation. 

His contribution, “Lolo House,” recreates a version of the home where he grew up. The installation is part recording studio, part performance space and part family archive.

Visitors are invited to step inside.

“I wanted to give people a visual representation of how my mind works,” Ortega said.

Inside are handwritten poems, musical instruments, family objects and original music. Rather than simply looking at art, visitors move through it, listen to it and become part of the experience.

“Making art has been lifesaving,” he said. “It helped me find myself, and I hope it encourages others to find their own creative expression. Through that liberation, there is revolution, and there is change.”

Near the end of the walkthrough, Tony Ortega returned to where the work began. 

“Our home became an incubator,” he said. “A place for not only family, love, togetherness, but of art-making.”

The post At BMoCA, three artists turn family history into a conversation across generations appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.

item.title: Boulder’s Spruce Pool will stay open in 2027. After that, its future is unclear.
item.dc:creator: Por Jaijongkit
item.description:
One-time funding will keep the longtime Whittier gathering place open for the 2027 season, but the city says no ongoing funding is available for 2028 as Boulder confronts rising costs and cuts across its recreation system.

The post Boulder’s Spruce Pool will stay open in 2027. After that, its future is unclear. appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.
item.content:encoded:
For more than a century, Spruce Pool has been a fixture in Boulder’s Whittier neighborhood. It is one of the city’s few public lap pools and a gathering place for a close-knit community of regulars.

Now, its future is uncertain.

The city manager’s newly released budget proposal, totaling about $550 million, would use about $134,000 in one-time funding to keep Spruce open through the summer of 2027. City staff have not decided to close the pool, but they say no ongoing funding currently exists to operate it beyond next year.

“For many of us, Spruce Pool means summer in Boulder,” said Lynn Stein, who has been swimming there for 32 years. She and other regulars said closing the pool would mean losing not only a place to exercise but also a community built over decades. 

“We understand that this can be very disappointing for community members,” said Scott Schuttenberg, deputy director of Boulder Parks and Recreation. He said the lack of continued funding “is not a reflection of the value of Spruce Pool.” 

The uncertainty over Spruce comes amid broader strain on Boulder’s recreation system. The city is trying to close a $6.3 million gap in its 2027 general fund as operating costs rise and tax revenue remains flat. It also faces roughly $400 million in unfunded repairs and replacements for aging public buildings, including its rec centers.

Voters will decide in November whether to authorize up to $400 million in city debt, repaid through higher property taxes, for major capital projects. But the measure’s passage is far from assured. A recent poll found that it lacked majority support.

Even if voters approve the Recreation and Safety Bond, the money could not cover recurring expenses such as lifeguard wages, utilities and pool chemicals. Spruce is not among the projects the city has identified for bond funding, and the measure would provide no money to operate it. The bond “does not address operational or ongoing dollars,” Schuttenberg said.

The budget pressures extend beyond Spruce. The recommended 2027 budget, released Aug. 28, would reduce hours at Scott Carpenter Pool outside the peak summer season, lay off 13 city employees, eliminate 11 vacant positions and cut other services. It would mark the third consecutive year of citywide budget reductions as Boulder contends with rising costs and sluggish revenue growth.

The Parks and Recreation Department has tried to bring in more money by raising fees and introducing a new membership program. But additional service reductions were expected in 2027 because expenses continued to outpace revenue.

A neighborhood gathering place

Spruce Pool began as an offshoot of the ice business next door. The Hygienic Ice and Coal Company built an enclosed swimming pool at Spruce and 21st streets in 1922, using warm water produced during ice manufacturing at its adjacent plant. Known as the Hygienic Swimming Pool, it opened the following year.

Historic photographs preserved by the Carnegie Library for Local History show children taking swimming lessons there, including classes sponsored by the Boulder School Board. The city bought the pool in 1950. In 1963, it demolished the enclosed building and reopened the site as the outdoor Spruce Pool.

Longtime swimmers said Spruce has become a gathering place that cannot be replicated at Boulder’s other pools. They described Scott Carpenter Pool as busier and more like a water park, with larger crowds, more amenities and difficult parking. Spruce, they said, is quieter and more conducive to conversation. Stein described it as an informal third place where people can catch up with friends without making plans in advance, particularly for Boulder retirees. 

The prospect of losing that community has alarmed regulars. 

“It’s a devastating loss to us,” said Mary Gorman, 73, who uses the pool for physical therapy and said it helped her reconnect with neighbors after the pandemic closures. 

Regulars said Spruce also tends to draw fewer competitive swimmers than Scott Carpenter, leaving more room for older adults, people recovering from surgery and residents with mobility limitations. Gorman said the pool is important to residents’ physical and mental health.

Other swimmers questioned the prospect of closing a public pool as Boulder’s summers grow hotter. They said Spruce can provide relief during hot weather, particularly for people without air conditioning at home. 

Schuttenberg said the city has no plans to sell the property, but some regulars worry that a closure could eventually lead to its sale.

“The value of Spruce is so much more than the dollars a developer is looking at,” said Deborah Fryer, another swimmer.

Stein and other residents said they hope to work with the city to find a way to keep the pool open.

Fewer visits, higher costs

Spruce’s operating costs have exceeded its revenue since it reopened in 2023, according to city staff. In 2025, the pool closed weeks before its traditional Labor Day closing date as the city sought to reduce costs. 

Spruce, which is much smaller than Scott Carpenter Pool, recorded about 15,000 visits in 2024, compared with 59,000 at Scott Carpenter.

That year, Spruce cost about $203,000 to operate and generated roughly $120,000 in revenue, leaving an $83,000 gap covered by what the city calls a “subsidy” from elsewhere in the Parks and Recreation system.

City spokesperson Kate Hernandez said the one-time $134,000 allocation from the general fund would cover the projected gap between the pool’s expenses and revenue in 2027.

“This subsidy is not something we can afford after 2027,” she said.

City staff said staffing, pool chemicals and utilities have also become more expensive. Gas and electricity for the pool cost about $9,600 in 2019. By 2024, that figure had more than tripled, to $32,900.

Schuttenberg said substantially raising admission prices was not a workable solution because Boulder already charges fees at the higher end of the market.

“It is a balancing act,” he said. Charge too much, he added, and fewer people use the facility, reducing revenue.

Keeping Spruce open beyond 2027 without a new source of money would likely require cuts elsewhere in Parks and Recreation, Schuttenberg said. He said the department has prioritized access for lower-income residents, older adults on fixed incomes, people with disabilities and children, along with basic park maintenance, including cleanliness and safety.

“Moving forward, there’s a lot of unknowns, but at this point we just don’t have the operating budget beyond 2027,” Schuttenberg said. He said he hoped the city would discuss possible new funding sources next year.

The recommended budget will undergo several public reviews. The city council is scheduled to discuss it at a study session on Sept. 10 and will hold public hearings on Oct. 1 and 15.

The Parks and Recreation Advisory Board is scheduled to review the budget and make a recommendation to the city council at its Sept. 28 meeting. Board Chair Andrew Bernstein said members were not briefed on the proposed loss of ongoing Spruce Pool funding before the budget was released publicly on Aug. 28. The board reviews the Parks and Recreation budget each year and recommends whether the city council should approve it.

“I’ve never seen a PRAB not recommend the budget,” Bernstein said. “However, this is the first time we’ve ever been asked to recommend a budget that includes service cuts.”

Brooke Stephenson contributed reporting to this story. 

The post Boulder’s Spruce Pool will stay open in 2027. After that, its future is unclear. appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.

item.title: Boulder Market Meals: Make summer tomatoes last with slow-roasted ‘candy’
item.dc:creator: John Lehndorff and Katie MacKinnon, Boulder County Farmers Markets
item.description:
Slow-roast cherry, grape and plum tomatoes with olive oil and herbs, then freeze them for pastas, salads, sandwiches and more.

The post Boulder Market Meals: Make summer tomatoes last with slow-roasted ‘candy’ appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.
item.content:encoded:
Market Meals is a collaboration between Boulder Reporting Lab and the Boulder County Farmers Markets, featuring weekly seasonal recipes built around ingredients from local growers, ranchers and food producers. Find it in Nibbles every Tuesday and on Boulder Reporting Lab. Sign up to get Nibbles in your inbox.

Eating with the seasons makes us hyper-aware of the passage of time. We count down the days until our favorite farmers market finds arrive. Then, suddenly, local growers tell us that those juicy peaches or beautiful dahlias will be available for only another week or two.

That rhythm encourages us to be present and to thoroughly enjoy what each season has to offer. It also gives us the opportunity to preserve each season’s goodies before we move on to what the next season brings. Preservation is an essential part of eating locally year-round, especially in a place that experiences all four seasons like Colorado.

Thankfully, we have excellent local resources, like Slow Food Boulder County and You Enjoy Life Homestead. Both organizations have visited the Boulder and Longmont markets to offer tips on making the tastes of summer last.

This week’s recipe from Slow Food Boulder County offers another way to preserve tomatoes. Rather than pickling, canning or simply freezing them, slowly roast cherry, plum, currant, pear and grape tomatoes into sweet, chewy bites you can enjoy through the holidays.

For further inspiration, check out Mountain Girl Pickles, Know Your Roots, Ferment Culture, or The Happy Pickle Company. These Boulder County vendors are experts in pickling and preservation with creative offerings like pickled garlic, kimchi and peach salsa.

Slow Food Tomato ‘Candy’

  • Tiny tomatoes (cherry, grape, plum, currant or pear)
  • Extra virgin olive oil
  • Dried herbs (such as basil, tarragon, thyme and chives)
  • Coarse sea salt

Slice the tomatoes in half. In a large bowl, toss them with a generous glug of olive oil, a sprinkling of dried herbs, and a pinch of salt. Arrange them cut side up in a single layer, face up, on a sheet pan lined with parchment paper. Bake at 220 degrees until the tomatoes are chewy, tender and lightly caramelized, about six to eight hours.

Add them to pasta, sandwiches or omelets, or use them to top grain bowls, salads and pizzas. Serve the oven-dried tomato candy with local goat cheese and crackers.

To store, divide the tomatoes into half-cup portions. Place them in pint jars or freezer bags, cover with olive oil and freeze. To serve, thaw them to room temperature or warm gently in a skillet over low heat.

What’s fresh this week? Farmers are bringing pears, melons, summer squash, potatoes, eggplant, peppers, sweet corn, tomatoes, green beans, okra, carrots, garlic, sugar snap peas, fennel, broccoli, fresh bouquets, meat, eggs and more to the Boulder and Longmont farmers markets this week.
